title: The quiet successor's words
hookLine: Guru Angad's saloks, short verses, sit inside the Vars

cards: Guru Nanak's voice fills raga after raga of the Guru Granth Sahib, hymn after long hymn.

Go looking for the second Guru's, and it arrives another way: in small pieces, a few lines each, tucked into the Vars, the ballads, between the stanzas. Each carries a small heading: Mahala two, the second voice.
This is Guru Angad, the disciple Guru Nanak chose to follow him, and in the stories about him, a man of few words and much service. The first thing to notice is how small each piece is.

teach.h: A SALOK: A FEW SHARP LINES.
teach.b: A salok is a short verse of a few lines, set in the Vars before the longer stanzas, like a sharp word before a speech. That's where Guru Angad's verses live. What can a few lines hold?
Here's one from the Var in Majh, the ballad this path just closed, in paraphrase. To see without eyes. To hear without ears.

teach.h: SEE WITHOUT EYES, WALK WITHOUT FEET.
teach.b: To walk without feet. To work without hands. To speak without a tongue.
This way, a person dies while still alive. Nanak, recognize the divine order, and meet your Master. Notice the signature: Nanak, though it's the second Guru speaking.
That's the name carrying on. And notice the form. Five short pictures, each impossible on its face, stacked one after another.
One line to turn them: this is dying while alive. One line to point the way: recognize the hukam.
Some Sikh teachers read it as a picture of living without ego: seeing, hearing, working and speaking, but no longer driven by the self that wants to own it all. The verse doesn't explain that.
It leaves the five pictures hanging and lets you work them out.
That's the quiet successor's style: something small and dense, the way a seed is small, left to open in you over a long time.
That's today's line: few words, deep.

how: Sikhs hear Guru Angad's saloks when the Vars are sung in kirtan, especially Asa di Var in the morning, where his saloks sit beside those of Guru Nanak.

games.q: what does “the quiet successor's words” mean?
o: a Guru's last words, passed to the next Guru
Guru Angad's short, dense verses inside the ballads
the silent prayers said by a Guru's successor

games.q: the salok's pictures: tap the pairs.

s: Guru Angad's verses fill whole sections of their own in the Granth
they come as saloks, short verses set inside the Vars, the ballads.
Guru Angad's salok is signed Nanak
the Gurus after Nanak whose verses are in the Granth signed with his name; the heading Mahala two marks this voice.
the salok ends by telling the listener to recognize the hukam
after the five pictures: this is dying while alive; recognize the order and meet the Master.

games.q: a salok gives five impossible pictures: see without eyes, hear without ears, walk without feet. what comes next?
o: one line: this is dying while alive.
a story about the Guru's life.
games.why: it doesn't explain them; it names them dying while alive, then points to recognizing the hukam.

practice: Take just one picture from the salok, whichever stays with you, hear without ears, maybe, or work without hands.
Keep that phrase in front of you as your breath slows, and turn it over the way you'd turn a stone in your palm, without trying to solve it. If you pray, say Waheguru on each breath out.

wordCard.voice: The quiet successor's words. Guru Angad's saloks, marked Mahala two, a few dense lines each, set inside the ballads of the Granth. Today's word.

orig.note: the heading that marks a verse as the second Guru's voice.

carryVoice: Your line: few words, deep. A seed is small, and it takes its time. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Guru Granth Sahib, Majh ki Var, salok Mahala 2, Ang 139 (see without eyes, hear without ears... thus die while alive; recognize the hukam)
